text.p: Channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel said on Tuesday it was heavily insured, but a spokesman was unable to comment on whether this would cover a fire last night on a shuttle train service.

"We are heavily insured, but the degree to which we are covered depends on the causes of the fire...The key thing now is to get a report on the incident to see whether we're insured for particular problems," he told Reuters.

French insurer UAP, which recently merged with Axa, was the leader on third party liability cover and insurance for damage to the tunnel and equipment. U.S. insurer Chubb Corp insures Eurotunnel's rolling stock, the spokesman said.
A spokeswoman for Chubb in London confirmed that the company "insured parts of the Eurotunnel organisation."

UAP also provides business interruption insurance which could be claimed against for the cost of business lost while the tunnel is closed. Eurotunnel said traffic would be cut to one third of normal levels after the fire swept through one of its main tunnels, adding that there was no fixed timescale on how long services would be reduced.
Eight people were hurt on Monday night after a fire broke out in a truck being transported on a freight shuttle train through the Channel Tunnel from Britain to France.

The 35 mile long (51 km) tunnnel was closed after the train, used to transport trucks and their drivers, was evacuated just after 2100 GMT with the carriages around 12 miles (19 km) from the French end of the tunnel.
Eurotunnel said it was the first time the tunnel had been closed for an emergency.
The Le Shuttle train involved in the fire was owned and operated by Eurotunnel.
No Eurostar passenger trains were involved in the incident, although their services have been disrupted by the tunnel's closure. Eurostar is a separate consortium.
All insurance claims will be handled via Eurotunnel's insurance brokers, Alexander & Alexander Services.
